---
title: "Why Serious Games Disappear"
description: "Evidence, system barriers and testable hypotheses about discontinuation"
---

## Non-availability is not necessarily abandonment

A research game may never be released publicly. A previously available game may stop working, lose distribution or become unsupported. The [availability audit](../games/availability.qmd) documents the access gap; it cannot determine which pathway caused each case.

Our **sustainability hypothesis** is that a brochure requires fewer interdependent forms of maintenance than a serious game. Games may need coordinated clinical, pedagogical, design and software expertise, plus distribution and user support. Losing a key contributor or grant may remove both operational ownership and undocumented knowledge. The contribution of these causes to type 1 diabetes (T1D) games has not been established.

## What adjacent research suggests

Healthcare sustainability reviews identify organisational capacity, funding, adaptation and implementation context as recurring influences ([Braithwaite et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-036453)). A digital-health review in low- and middle-income countries also identifies technical and infrastructure constraints; its setting limits direct transfer to T1D-game projects elsewhere ([Kaboré et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.3389/fdgth.2022.1014375)).

Research-software work describes a mismatch between incentives for novel outputs and recognition or funding for maintenance ([Anzt et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.23224.1)). In an observational analysis of more than 36,000 open-source projects, 89% had lost their core development team at least once and 27% of abandoned projects attracted a new core developer. These findings concern software generally, not health games; recruiting a successor is not proof of sustained recovery ([Nourry et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1587/transinf.2025EDL8005)).

## Plausible failure mechanisms to investigate

| Mechanism | Evidence needed in a particular project |
|---|---|
| Funding ends at publication | Development, hosting, support and update budgets before and after the study |
| Expertise or authority leaves | Contributor history, ownership of accounts, handover records and ability of a successor to release |
| A dependency becomes unavailable | Build failures, retired services, hardware or store requirements |
| Content and software versions diverge | Which release the clinical review, translation and outcome evidence apply to |
| The product does not fit care delivery | Staff time, referral workflow, language, age and supervision requirements |
| Users or clinicians cannot assess trustworthiness | Discoverability, accountable ownership, privacy information and traceable claims |

These are hypotheses and investigative questions, not measured frequencies in T1D games. Operational responses belong in [maintenance patterns](maintenance-patterns.qmd).

## Why a game may not be offered at diagnosis

Availability alone does not create an education pathway. A product must also fit the person's age, language, learning needs and available devices, and the clinic must know when and how to introduce it. A supervised paediatric study cannot establish suitability for an unsupervised newly diagnosed adult.

Uncertain ownership, unclear evaluation and staff effort are plausible adoption barriers supported indirectly by the implementation literature above. Their relevance to an individual clinic requires local investigation. This knowledge base cannot explain why any particular person received—or did not receive—a game during diagnosis education.

## Research that would distinguish the causes

Follow research-origin games longitudinally from study completion: distinguish never released, released but inaccessible, supported, archived and replaced. Interview developers and educators about costs, staff turnover, handover and referral decisions. Compare those histories with actual releases and usage rather than attributing disappearance to the end of funding by default.

Open evidence, documented design and reusable software may reduce reconstruction work for successors. Whether this improves T1D-game survival is a testable proposition, not an established benefit of this knowledge base.
